A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCBM research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including the additional hard-CBM appendix in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original leakage, concept-accuracy, alignment, disentanglement, and toy intervention experiments in Section 5.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments in Section 4, including leakage measurements, task and concept accuracy, representation analyses, and intervention-error curves.

M1.justification: The representation head, conditional-information regularizer, combined training objective, prototype-based interventions, and noise conventions are retained. Appendix C's training algorithm is unchanged. The new hard-CBM treatment describes comparison methods rather than a new MCBM component.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 changes from animal-versus-vehicle classification with eight class concepts and two excluded classes to standard ten-class classification using 64 of 143 semantic attributes. CelebA's gender/attribute evaluation is removed. MPI3D, Shapes3D, CUB, and the spiral scenario remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds ARCBM and SCBM to the leakage, concept-accuracy, and representation comparisons previously involving CBM, CEM, and the applicable Vanilla baseline. These additions substantially broaden comparison against leakage-mitigation alternatives. Figure 5 labels one intervention curve HCBM while its accompanying text names SCBM, leaving that curve's precise identity uncertain.

E3.justification: The hyperparameter tables change CIFAR-10 from ResNet20, 50 epochs, and SGD to two convolutional layers, 200 epochs, and Adam. CUB changes from seven to twelve concept groups and revises its gamma values, although v2 inconsistently retains '20 remaining' groups out of 27. v2 also introduces task-accuracy evaluation and an intervention protocol measuring error while correcting progressively more lowest-confidence concepts.

E4.justification: v1's toy CIFAR leakage and class-substitution intervention analyses disappear. v2 adds systematic intervention analysis on CIFAR-10 and CUB, examines the task-accuracy cost across gamma values, and adds a bimodal-prior illustration of the sigmoid-inverse problem. The nuisance-removal, concept-preservation, and spiral analyses remain; regrouping the existing spiral plots is not new experimental evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report average values with plus/minus quantities without defining their statistical meaning or specifying run counts, seeds, or confidence levels. Additional result rows and revised numerical spreads do not establish a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds task-accuracy results and intervention-error curves, expands comparator results, and revises alignment and disentanglement values. Under the retained Shapes3D setting, CBM task-related URR changes from 8.1 ± 2.9 in v1 Table 2 to 18.1 ± 2.9 in v2 Table 3. CelebA results disappear, while CIFAR results use a different task. Changed CUB settings also prevent interpreting its revised scores as direct performance gains.

T1.justification: The core MCBM information objectives and Appendix B derivations remain unchanged. New Appendix D adds a supporting mathematical treatment of hard CBMs: a prediction-level conditional-information objective, probability factorization, Heaviside binarization, and intervention formulation in Equations 24–27.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims that CBMs do not exclude nuisance information and that MCBMs use a variational information bottleneck to preserve concepts, improve interpretability, and enable principled interventions. The revised abstract and conclusion shift emphasis without changing the underlying contributions.

C2.justification: v2 develops the distinction between removing nuisances from representations and imposing a hard bottleneck before prediction, explaining why interventions can improve without making latent representations interpretable. It adds interpretations of intervention behavior across gamma values and comparative task-accuracy costs. Its task-related leakage discussion also qualifies v1's claim that CEMs always retain more nuisances than Vanilla models to a generally observed tendency.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository pointer and documents GPT-3 attribute construction and CLIP-based positive/negative attribute assignment for the revised CIFAR setup. Its hyperparameter table updates CIFAR and CUB settings and removes CelebA details. The training pseudocode and most existing implementation documentation are retained.

R1.justification: v2 removes the dedicated disentanglement taxonomy and discussions of GlanceNets and several CEM variants. It instead develops positioning against hard, autoregressive, and stochastic CBMs, expanding the role of the already-cited Havasi work. New references include stochastic CBMs, intervention-selection research, and the sources supporting semantic-attribute construction. This substantively changes the related-work framing.

P1.justification: The introduction and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. v1's separate modeling and bottleneck sections are consolidated into v2 Section 2, related work moves afterward, and intervention criticisms and the spiral discussion are assembled into Section 5. The appendices are extended and reorganized around the new hard-CBM treatment.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual summary table and diagram, task-accuracy table, intervention curves, prior-density plot, and hard-CBM graphical model. It removes the toy CIFAR plots, merges v1 Figures 6–8 into one spiral figure, expands comparison tables and heatmaps, and recolors existing graphical models. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v2's task-accuracy table and systematic intervention curves address empirical gaps left by v1's leakage-focused evaluation and toy intervention example. The added comparators and clearer distinction between representation and prediction bottlenecks strengthen assessment of the central claims. These gains are tempered by the loss of CelebA coverage and new reporting inconsistencies, particularly CUB's incompatible group counts and the SCBM/HCBM labeling mismatch. The net improvement is supported but limited.
